title: Good Friday
hookLine: John's passion, prayers for the whole world, and the veneration of the cross
carry: behold the wood of the cross

cards: Three o'clock on a Friday afternoon. People in the pews, and almost no sound. The altar is bare.

No bells, no opening song. The priest and ministers walk in without a word, and then the priest does something you won't see on an ordinary Sunday: he lies face down on the floor, or kneels, and stays there in silence.
Nobody explains it. Everyone waits. Today, in the Roman Rite, there is no Mass at all.

teach.b: The service, often at three in the afternoon, the hour Jesus died, has three parts.
First, the readings: Isaiah's suffering servant, wounded for our iniquities, and then, every year, the Passion from John's gospel, often read in parts. John's Jesus is strikingly calm.
In the garden, when the soldiers come, he steps forward and says, I am he, and they fall back. He carries his own cross. From it he gives his mother and his beloved disciple to each other.
And his last words, in the Douay-Rheims, are: "It is consummated." Finished, completed, the work done.
Then the second part, the Solemn Intercessions: ten long prayers for the whole world.

For the Church and the pope, for those preparing for baptism, for Christian unity, for the Jewish people, for those who don't believe in Christ or in God, for leaders, and for everyone who suffers. Nobody is left out.
A cross is carried up the aisle, unveiled in stages or carried in procession, and the priest sings in the old Latin: "Ecce lignum Crucis."

teach.h: BEHOLD THE WOOD OF THE CROSS.
teach.b: Behold the wood of the cross, on which hung the salvation of the world. Come, let us adore. And people come forward one by one to genuflect, touch, or kiss the wood.
Communion follows, from hosts consecrated the night before, and everyone leaves in silence. Catholics fast today. And why call it good?
Some say the word once carried a sense close to holy. Catholics call it good because of what they believe was finished on the cross.

how: On Good Friday Catholics celebrate the Passion of the Lord, often at 3 p.m., with John's Passion, the Solemn Intercessions, the veneration of the cross and Communion; no Mass is celebrated, and it is a day of fasting and abstinence.

games.q: you're at the veneration. the cross has been unveiled and the line moves forward. what do people do when they reach it?
o: genuflect, touch, or kiss the wood.
games.why: one by one they genuflect, touch or kiss the cross. the Alleluia stays silent until Easter.

practice: If there's a crucifix in your home, a cross on a chain, or one in a church you can reach, hold it, touch it or kiss it the way people do at the veneration; if you have none, trace one on your palm with a finger.
Then sit in silence, the way the church does today, and let it be heavy if it's heavy. If you pray, whisper the old words, behold the wood of the cross; if you don't, simply stay with the silence.

wordCard.voice: Good Friday. The day of the Lord's Passion: no Mass, John's Passion, prayers for the whole world, and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: behold the wood of the cross, sung as the cross is shown on Good Friday.
